claims.text: High-energy ball milling under argon followed by vacuum spark plasma sintering produces finer grains than conventional melting.
This processing route produces a more uniform dispersion of secondary phases or precipitates than conventional processing.
The refined and more uniform microstructure governs increased hardness and strength.
A conventionally melted baseline alloy has a coarser grain structure.
A conventionally melted baseline alloy has a less uniform dispersion of second phases.
Mechanical milling introduces severe plastic deformation.
Mechanical milling creates high defect densities.
Consolidation by rapid spark plasma sintering results in significant grain refinement.
Mechanical milling followed by spark plasma sintering creates a uniform dispersion of strengthening phases.
Refined grain boundaries increase resistance to dislocation motion through grain-boundary strengthening.
Dispersed precipitates or inclusions increase resistance to dislocation motion through precipitate hardening.
Increased resistance to dislocation motion enhances hardness and strength.
The ball-milled and spark-plasma-sintered alloy will have higher hardness than the conventionally processed baseline.
The ball-milled and spark-plasma-sintered alloy will have higher strength than the conventionally processed baseline.
SEM or TEM will reveal finer grains and uniformly dispersed nanoscale strengthening features in the processed alloy.
The proposed behavior is expected to apply primarily to high-entropy alloys that form single-phase solid solutions.
Processing-induced contamination can invalidate the proposed behavior.
Unwanted processing-induced phase transformations can invalidate the proposed behavior.
Intrinsic multiphase microstructures can dominate the mechanical response and invalidate the proposed behavior.
Variability in milling energy, sintering dynamics, contamination, and alloy sensitivity makes the enhancement magnitude uncertain.

contradictions.description: The mechanism relies partly on dispersed secondary phases or precipitates, while the stated applicability is primarily to single-phase solid-solution alloys. The hypothesis does not clarify whether these nanoscale features preserve the intended single-phase regime or constitute a multiphase state excluded by the boundary.
